doc.title: Claude Williams interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Florida dance segregation and how Count Basie hired him
summary: He recalls segregated dances, Basie's Reno Club broadcasts, John Hammond, Nat Cole's brother's Chicago band, and Basie picking him up to enlarge the band.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: MR: I’d like you to ask him, just so we have it on tape, some of the early stories about traveling down to Florida, and how that worked with the money they were making and them being picked up, and how the Count came to find you, and just a little bit about that?

Yeah well we’re jumping a long ways. Different times we’d have down in Florida — you know that was down south and quite segregated then, you know. And we played some dances for whites that the colored couldn’t go to, and then we played some for colored that they wouldn’t let the whites go to down south. They were all messed up like that. Like I say I heard Joe Venuti. I was standing almost about a block, at least a half a block from the pavilion, about as close as I could get to him, and he was in my home town in Muskogee then. And let’s see that was down there. Oh, I knew Count before, you know Count came to Kansas City way before he ever had a chance to get him a group together we used to jam, we’d jam up and down the street there. And when the Count had been playing with Bennie Moten and Bennie Moten had got killed. He and the doctor was out partying all night and he went to have his tonsils taken out and never did wake up on the table. Well that doctor left Kansas City. I don’t know what ever happened to him. And then so Bennie Moten’s band broke up down to, Count was playing with Bennie then so Count just picked a few people that he wanted, you know, and started a small group there in a joint called Reno there in Kansas City. And he picked like him, the drummer, and bass, Walter Page they called “Big ‘Un” he was in the Blue Devils — the Blue Devils had just broke up too about a year before then. So Count picked out a rhythm section and some, one or two saxophones or something like that, and was playing at this Reno Club there in Kansas City where they broadcast every night. It was such a strong station, I never will forget that W9XVY. It was a station you could hear just as good in New York as you could in Kansas City. So what happened, they broadcast every night from twelve to twelve thirty, or twelve thirty to one, something like that. And I hear Benny Goodman picked up the thing one night. And Benny told his brother-in-law which was John Hammond about the group, and John Hammond checked it and he went down to Kansas City and listened to it. In the meantime he was delighted with what he heard, and he laid some cash on Count for him to get him to enlarge his band. And I had been around Chicago playing. I played with Nat Cole and his brother had a band there. And King was, he was the best piano player in Chicago then, but he didn’t know he could sing. He didn’t even try to sing, he just played good piano. So a little thing happened and I didn’t stay with them very long, so I was back in Chicago and Count heard that I was up there and he came up and picked me up and went back to Kansas City to enlarge his band. He enlarged it up to I think twelve or thirteen pieces. At that time Herschel was out there in California, Lester was there, Big ‘Un was there, and oh the trumpet player, what they

called Hot Lips Page, he was there. See he had two different bands I think to pick from because the Blue Devils had broke up and there was some of them which — Hot Lips and Walter Page was the Blue Devils and Lester came up there with the Blue Devils, and so he really didn’t have too much more after he got me to finish out the rhythm section. And Buck Clayton just happened to come through because Buck lived in Parsons, Kansas and he’d been living out here in L.A. So that’s what happened with me joining Count.
